extracted.intended_audience: postsecondary institutions' Title IX coordinators, administrators, investigators, decisionmakers, and legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and implementing §106.46 grievance procedures for postsecondary institutions, with particular rules for live questioning, individual meetings, evidence access, and methods for assessing credibility consistent with the final Title IX regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-questioning process to assess credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance procedure requirements in §106.46 will include a live-questioning process that enables the decisionmaker to assess credibility of parties and witnesses to the extent credibility is both in dispute and relevant to one or more allegations of sex-based harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a baseline requirement: institutions must adopt a process that allows a decisionmaker to evaluate credibility where credibility matters to the allegations. The live-questioning process is intended to produce reliable outcomes while protecting parties' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible forms of live questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Live questioning, including questions and follow-up questions proposed by the parties, could occur in individual meetings with the investigator or decisionmaker, or in a live hearing with questions asked by the decisionmaker or the party's advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may choose either individual-meeting (inquisitorial-style) procedures or live-hearing (adversarial-style) procedures, or offer both as circumstances warrant. The regulations permit flexibility to select the form best suited to the facts, resources, and legal obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties may propose questions but need not personally ask them
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department's procedures allow for live questioning, including questions proposed by respondents themselves but asked by the decisionmaker or an advisor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties should be able to submit proposed questions and follow-ups; the institution ensures the questions are posed by an investigator, the decisionmaker, or the party's advisor consistent with the method chosen. This balances respondents' interests in challenging credibility with protections against direct harassment of complainants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on permissible questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions proposed by the parties must be relevant and not otherwise impermissible under §§106.2 and 106.45(b)(7) and may not be unclear or harassing under §106.46(f)(3); credibility questions about a complainant's sexual history must comply with §106.45(b)(7)(iii).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisionmakers/investigators must screen proposed questions for relevance and impermissibility before posing them. Institutions may decline to ask questions that are duplicative, harassing, unclear, or barred by evidentiary limits (e.g., sexual-history restrictions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordings/transcripts and opportunity for follow-up when no live hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: When a postsecondary institution chooses not to hold a live hearing, the process must provide each party with an audio or audiovisual recording or transcript of the individual meetings with enough time for the party to have a reasonable opportunity to propose follow-up questions (§106.46(f)(1)(i)(C)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide timely recordings/transcripts of individual meetings and allow parties to propose follow-up questions after reviewing them. This requirement is intended to approximate the opportunity to respond that live questioning affords and to ensure fairness even outside a live hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number and timing of individual meetings
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be one or more individual meetings, including follow-up meetings with the parties and witnesses, as needed to establish facts, assess credibility, and ask follow-up questions; the appropriate number varies with the facts and proposed questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not set a fixed number of meetings; permit additional meetings where necessary but decline further meetings if proposed follow-ups are duplicative, harassing, or otherwise improper. The process should avoid an 'endless cycle' while ensuring adequate opportunity to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may conduct individual meetings and whether they may be virtual
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual meetings may be conducted by the investigator, decisionmaker, or both, at the institution's discretion, and nothing precludes conducting such meetings virtually with technology that enables parties to simultaneously see and hear one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may choose whether investigators, decisionmakers, or both attend individual meetings; for panels, institutions decide whether the whole panel must be present. Virtual meetings are allowed provided the technology facilitates live interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of individual-meeting information in the evidentiary record
rubrics_metrics.description: The information gathered at individual meetings with parties and witnesses would be part of the evidence or investigative report covered under §106.46(e)(6)(i), and parties must have an opportunity to review and respond prior to the determination whether sex-based harassment occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat statements from individual meetings as part of the evidence. Provide parties equal access to relevant, not-impermissible evidence or to an investigative report that accurately summarizes that evidence, and give a reasonable opportunity to respond per §106.46(e)(6)(ii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker must screen questions for relevance before posing
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.46(f)(3) the decisionmaker must determine before the question is posed whether a question proposed by the parties is relevant and not otherwise impermissible under §§106.2 and 106.45(b)(7) or unclear or harassing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The institution's adopted process must ensure the decisionmaker performs this pre-posing relevance and permissibility determination; this is a procedural safeguard against abusive or irrelevant questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live-hearing options for assessing credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When a postsecondary institution chooses to conduct a live hearing under §106.46(g), the process must allow the decisionmaker to ask relevant and not otherwise impermissible questions and either: (a) allow each party to propose such questions to be asked by the decisionmaker, or (b) allow each party's advisor to ask such questions as long as they are not unclear or harassing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live hearings are not required, but if used the institution must permit one of these two methods for conducting questioning. Institutions are not required to permit advisor-conducted questioning in every case; they can permit decisionmaker-asked party-proposed questions instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency requirement within resolution of a particular complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent a party's need for a disability or language-access accommodation or provision of auxiliary aids/services, an institution must use the same method for assessing credibility for each party or witness within resolution of a particular complaint because grievance procedures must be fair and treat the parties equitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may vary methods between different complaints, but must articulate consistent principles in their written grievance procedures explaining when and why one method will be used over another (e.g., advisor questioning where potential sanction is suspension/expulsion). This ensures predictability and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion to choose live hearings or other procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in §106.46(f)(1) or elsewhere in the final regulations precludes a postsecondary institution from choosing to use a live hearing with questioning by an advisor, either because it is required under applicable Federal or State case law or for any other reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions retain discretion to maintain processes (including those from the 2020 amendments) that they determine better satisfy legal obligations or institutional values; the final regulations set baseline requirements, not a ceiling for procedural protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodation of competing interests in procedural design (Mathews factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department considered Mathews factors—the risk of erroneous deprivation and benefit of additional procedures, interests at stake for respondents and complainants, and the government's interest including burden and cost—in designing the live-questioning requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When crafting procedures, institutions should balance the interests in accurate outcomes and protection from re-traumatization against administrative and financial burdens. The chosen procedures should be tailored and justified in light of these considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness requirement despite not being a trial
rubrics_metrics.description: School disciplinary proceedings are not civil or criminal trials and need not provide the same panoply of procedural requirements, but basic principles of fairness require a live-questioning process that enables the decisionmaker to adequately assess credibility and provides a meaningful opportunity to respond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should avoid transplanting full criminal/civil trial procedures wholesale; instead, ensure baseline fairness features (notice, opportunity to respond, means to assess credibility) are preserved in a way appropriate to educational contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on abusive or repetitive questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: If follow-up questions proposed by a party are duplicative of questions already asked or designed to harass rather than assess credibility or elicit relevant information, the postsecondary institution may decline to hold additional meetings to ask the questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should document reasons for declining further questioning (e.g., duplication, harassment) and apply §106.2, §106.45(b)(7), and §106.46(f) standards consistently to prevent abuse of the process.
